candidates.source_body_excerpt: Regulator also vetoes extra Blackpool service, citing lack of space on west coast mainline for new trains to capital Plans to run direct train services to Wrexham and Rochdale from London have been rejected by the rail regulator because of “significant pressure” on the line. The Office of Rail and Road said that there was insufficient space on the crowded west coast mainline to introduce the two new separate train services. It also vetoed plans for additional London-Blackpool train services wanted by Avanti. The ORR had last year knocked back plans for a new independent open access service linking Wrexham and the capital put forward by the Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR). WSMR had submitted plans for a slightly less frequent service but the ORR said the new routes would still put the reliability of the wider railway at risk. The new service could have allowed Wrexham to capitalise further on the town’s Hollywood-meets-football mini-boom, fuelled by the Wrexham AFC co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. Proposals for a new Lumo service between London and Rochdale, again slimmed down after being rejected in 2025, were once more rebuffed. The ORR also said Avanti could not add more Blackpool services from London. However, it did approve one extra London-Chester evening service from Avanti, which would otherwise have run as a “ghost train”, with crew and the rolling stock returning north to the depot overnight. The decision follows the outcry over the ORR’s initial ruling on a Manchester-London service which was barred from taking passengers last year.

His next of kin were informed and are being supported by specialist officers.The victim was named locally as John McGarry, understood to have been 56, a father and a Rochdale AFC supporter, according to the Manchester Evening News. Tributes were posted by friends and others who said they were shocked by his death.One woman wrote:"So gutted fly high mate."Another person wrote:"So sad r.i.p John."A third person wrote:"What a horror condolences to the Mcgarry family x"A man who said he was one of McGarry's good friends wrote:"One my good friends r.ip pal up the dale shocked"Another person wrote:"Sad news fly high John."A man who said he had known McGarry for more than 40 years described him as a gentle and well-known figure in the area."He was a gentle giant, he was a tall lad. We used to go school with him, he was a really, really nice gentleman." he said.He added that people who had grown up in the area were discussing the death and expressing their shock."We've grown up around here, everyone knew him and we've been talking about how shocked we are. Officers were keeping an open mind and exploring all lines of inquiry.Police said the scene on Curzon Road would remain in place for several days, with an increased police presence in the area during the investigation."Anyone with information regarding this incident is urged to get in touch with police on 101 and quote log 3344 of 07/10/2026, or you can make a report via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk Alternatively contact Crimestoppers, anonymously, on 0800 555 111." candidates.source_body_excerpt: Bury North MP James Frith visited a housing development in Walmersley to meet an award winning site manager recognised for national construction standards. The visit took place at Barratt Homes’ Waldmers Wood development on Walmersley Old Road, where the MP met site manager Sean O’Regan. Mr O’Regan received both a Pride in the Job Quality Award and a Seal of Excellence from the National House Building Council in 2025, recognising the standards achieved on the development. During the visit, Mr Frith was given a tour of the site by Barratt Homes representatives including managing director Rhys Nicholson, construction director John McNulty and sales director Alan Watt. The visit included an overview of the construction progress and the energy efficient features being built into the homes. The development includes a mix of two, three and four bedroom properties, including apartments and lower cost homes. A total of 268 homes are planned for the site, with 33 designated as affordable housing as part of the planning agreement. Barratt Homes has also committed £156000 towards local community investment to support services and facilities in the surrounding area. James Frith MP said “Visiting Waldmers Wood was a great opportunity to see first hand the high quality homes being delivered here in Bury and to meet the dedicated team behind them. I was especially pleased to congratulate Sean on his well deserved national recognition which reflects the pride and professionalism going into this development. “Schemes like this are vital to helping more people access high quality modern and energy efficient homes. Too many first time buyers feel locked out of the market not because they cannot afford monthly repayments but because they do not have access to large deposits or family support. That has to change.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: An album featuring local artists’ versions of songs recorded in Rochdale has received national radio airplay following its release this summer. Kenion Street features 11 tracks originally recorded at Cargo or Suite Sixteen studios, performed by acts from the borough. Released on vinyl and digital platforms as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album includes PoolEra’s version of OMD’s Electricity, Medley performing New Order’s Dreams Never End and Jennifer Read covering The Fall’s Totally Wired. The recordings were produced by Jamie Alsop at Voltalab Sound Studios, which occupies the original Cargo and Suite Sixteen building on Kenion Street. Between 1977 and 2001, the studios hosted artists including Joy Division, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre and A Certain Ratio. Middleton band K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods received airplay on BBC Radio 6 Music and was named Track of the Day on Radio X. Organisers said tracks also featured on XS Manchester, Mersey Radio and Phoenix FM, among other stations. Listening parties took place at Rough Trade shops in London, Liverpool, Bristol and Nottingham, with vinyl copies distributed to record shops nationwide.

David said: “I've gone from having all the pieces of the puzzle to having something we can put into the hands of real people, test and develop, and which could ultimately help millions of people facing the same communication barriers that I've experienced myself.” BUILD AI was developed by the university’s Centre for Sustainable Innovation and delivered with NoCodeLab.ai. The six-week programme combined practical AI development with mentoring and support to explore how participants’ ideas could become products and businesses. The university said its 12 participants had brought four products to launch or near-launch, put six working prototypes into testing and developed two existing technology ventures.

Detective Sergeant Hannah Taala, from GMP’s Rochdale district, said: "This day has been months in the planning and I am delighted with the results that have already come in. We have arrested multiple people suspected of being involved in a range of offences, including drug-dealing, robberies, burglaries, and assaults. "This cycle of violence stops here. We have been able to strike a significant blow against a group that has been causing misery across the Rochdale district. People have asked us to tackle the issue and that’s exactly what we’ve done. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Eric Cantona, the M62 and the Industrial Revolution. Despite the long animosity between Lancashire and Yorkshire a few things have successfully made the journey across the Pennines. And to that list you can add the 590 bus . The Rochdale to Halifax service swaps the Roch Valley for the Calder Valley as it crosses over from Greater Manchester into West Yorkshire. And along the way it takes in two marvels of the Industrial Revolution and plenty of the region's most dramatic scenery. I caught the 590 this week as far as Hebden Bridge as part of our occasional series on Greater Manchester's most scenic bus routes . Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The first thing to note is because this is a privately-owned First Bus and not a publicly-controlled Bee Network service a single ticket is £2.50 not two quid. Having stumped up the extra 10 bob, I head upstairs to join a handful of students heading home after lectures on the top deck. From Rochdale bus station it heads east out of the town centre through Smallbridge and Littleborough before crossing the border at Summit into the towns of Walsden, Todmorden and Hebden Bridge. It's a pretty unremarkable start to the journey, but soon the chicken shops and rows of brick terraces start to give way to old weavers cottages and Rochdale's famous flagstone fences. Up ahead the dramatic gritstone ridge of Blackstone Edge, marking the border between Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, looms on the horizon. At Littleborough the bus turns north and as we begin the head into the hills we pass the former studio of the late Walter Kershaw. The painter was dubbed the 'Original Banksy' for his huge street murals and through the dusty bay window a number of his canvases can be seen still hung on the wall. At the crest of the hill, at the aptly-named village of Summit, we pass the mouth of the Summit Tunnel, a George Stephenson-designed miracle of Victorian engineering. When it opened in 1841, providing a direct link between the industrial powerhouses of Manchester and Leeds, it was the longest railway tunnel in the world. In 1984 it was also the scene of one of the biggest underground fires in transport history when a train carrying a million litres of petrol derailed. As temperatures inside reached a staggering 1,500C it took firefighters four days to extinguish the blaze. And it’s not the only reminder of our ancestors’ ingenuity along the route. To the right the Rochdale Canal, which opened 37 years before the tunnel, follows the same path along the valley. In years gone by hundreds of barges would have transported cotton, wool, coal and timber between Lancashire and Yorkshire. Today you’re much more likely to see a few pleasure cruisers eking out the last of the summer or, as I did near Walsden, a group of kayakers going for a paddle. As we approach the border with Yorkshire we also get a glimpse of a herd of alpacas, a long way from their native South America, grazing in a field of the far bank of the canal. But this is not some Cotswolds-style, AirBnB-filled theme park. Rochdale Council has received an application for the Burger Box, at the former Haibat Sultan restaurant at 26 Milkstone Road, to stay open until 3am daily. The Burger Box is described as a fast-food restaurant in a ground-floor retail unit with residential accommodation above, situated on a busy main road. Planning permission has been granted for eat-in, collection and delivery service from 11am to 11pm Monday to Sunday, and 11am to 10pm on Sundays and bank holidays. The licensing application looks to extend this to 3am each day. Under the terms of the premises licence, no alcohol can be taken into or be consumed in the restaurant at any time. Among the objections, Mrs S Rana believes that that there will be an increase in anti-social behaviour and noise from the restaurant. She is also concerned that there will be an increase in traffic and pollution if the licence is granted until 3am. Mr I Hussain believes the premises may attract anti-social behaviour within the area and lead to an increase of crime and disorder. He has concerns that the premises will create a public nuisance to residents especially with the late-night hours. He believes the licence should end at 11pm.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: 'Rochdale's Chernobyl' is a step closer to redevelopment after landowners appointed a specialist contractor to clean up the notorious former asbestos factory site. Decaying, dangerous and eerie are all words that would accurately describe the former Turner Brothers factory in the Spotland area of Rochdale. It used to be the world’s largest asbestos manufacturer and once employed thousands in the town, but it has sat empty for decades. It is off-limits to the public and only foolhardy ‘urban explorers’ dare trespass onto the site nicknamed ‘Rochdale’s Chernobyl’. Locally, there has been a long-held ambition to see the site bulldozed and brought back into use for the good of the community. Many locals would like to see the site transformed into a park that blends with the surrounding greenery. But the numerous redevelopment schemes have all included housing as well as various ideas for public open spaces. After a number of failed attempts at redevelopment, Spodden Park Ltd are the latest to try their hand at bringing the 75-acre site back into use. Although their future vision for the area off Spod Road has not been revealed, it is understood there is an ambition to build housing and create a park in some capacity. No details have been confirmed by the landowner, but they have outlined that the number of houses planned would be far fewer than the 650 previously touted in the 2000s. Spodden Park Limited took control of the site from ESG Trading Limited in 2024, but they’ve been slow to table their vision. They’ve previously explained that this is because they want to do things as safely as possible. This is understandable considering the carcinogenic nature of the asbestos previously produced on site. Their latest announcement is the appointment of a specialist contractor to carry out remediation work on the site. It is understood that once this is completed, the former asbestos production site will actually become viable for development.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Saturday saw Saints make the trip to Rochdale Rugby Club, perched on the edge of the Pennines, for their second game of the season. A fine, bright, warm day and a good pitch greeted the visitors. Injuries continue to affect Saints early in the campaign, with another three regular starters unavailable, although it was a welcome boost to see Oscar Crow and Niall Grant return on the bench. Saints made the early running, but Rochdale’s determined scrambling defence held firm until winger Sam Cotgrave barged his way over in the corner. Smith added the conversion while on kicking duties for the day. Rochdale then began to grow into the game, and with Smith shown a yellow card, the hosts took advantage. A well-worked try following missed tackles in the centre was converted to level the scores at 7-7. Rochdale missed several further scoring opportunities through dropped balls and a forward pass before eventually finding space to score beneath the posts, with the conversion giving them a 14-7 lead in front of a vocal home crowd. Saints responded well. After a penalty was kicked to touch six metres out, the resulting drive towards the line saw Joe Sanders cross for a try, with Ben Jones converting to make it 14-14. Saints continued to apply pressure, but Rochdale resisted until Olly Dodd sidestepped his defender and crossed on the stroke of half-time. Smith added the conversion on his return from the sin bin to give Saints a 21-14 lead at the break. Saints started the second half strongly, but a forced pass was spilled and Rochdale pounced, racing over in the corner. The conversion was missed, reducing the deficit to 21-19. The visitors quickly regained control. Changes in personnel helped Saints gain the upper hand in the scrum, which was beginning to take its toll on the Rochdale pack. After another attack close to the line, prop John Whittaker was driven over for a converted try, extending the lead to 28-19 and securing a bonus point. Saints were beginning to dominate possession, although Rochdale’s defence remained stubborn. A powerful scrum drive 10 metres out allowed Kincart to find Cotgrave, who slipped around his defender to score his second try of the afternoon. The conversion made it 35-19. Rochdale continued to throw everything into the contest. They were held up over the line before taking a quick tap penalty from an earlier offside offence, catching the Saints defence napping to score. The conversion was missed, but the hosts earned a deserved bonus point as the score moved to 35-24. Saints had the final say. Captain Will Grebe powered towards the line and, despite being tackled, somehow stretched out to ground the ball and score. The conversion was missed, but it completed a 40-24 victory for the visitors. It was not Saints’ best performance and they have yet to field a full-strength squad this season, but an away win and five league points represented a productive afternoon. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Police seized 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and found three cannabis farms after stopping a vehicle in Middleton on Sunday, October 4. A 38-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A drugs. Officers from Middleton’s Neighbourhood Policing Team spotted a vehicle they considered suspicious parked on Cemetery Street while on patrol. Greater Manchester Police said a search of the vehicle uncovered a quantity of Class A drugs, scales and cash. Following the arrest, further intelligence led officers to two addresses in Middleton and one in Chadderton, Oldham. Police found a cannabis farm at each address and recovered 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine during the searches. GMP estimated the suspected cocaine’s potential street value at around £2 million. The recovered substances are awaiting further assessment. The arrested man remained in custody for questioning when police issued their update.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: SATURDAY saw Saints make the trip to Rochdale Rugby Club perched on the edge of the Pennines. A fine bright warm day and good pitch greeted the visitors for the second game of the season with injuries again blighting the squad with three regular starters missing but the return of Oscar Crow and Niall Grant on the bench. From the start it was Saints going forward but the solid, scrambling defence of Rochdale held firm until winger Sam Cotgrave barged his way into the corner, converted by Billy Smith who was on kicking duties. Rochdale then really started to find their way into the game with Saints player Smith yellow carded, firstly with a well worked try after missed tackles in the centre converted to make the score 7-7. Rochdale wasted three more try scoring opportunities with a couple of dropped balls and a forward pass, until finally finding space to score under the posts converted for a 14-7 lead in front of a vocal home crowd. Saints pressed again and a penalty to touch six metres out was driven towards the line where Joe Sanders went over with Ben Jones converting to bring it back to 14-14. Again Saints piled on the pressure but Rochdale held firm until Olly Dodd sidestepped the defender before going over the whitewash on the stroke of halftime converted by Smith on his yellow card return. It was Saints who came out straight into attack but a forced pass was spilled and pounced on by Rochdale who raced over in the corner to pull it back to 19-21 as the conversion was missed.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Middleton could have two adult gaming arcades within feet of each other if new plans get the green light. JR Planning Consultants has applied to Rochdale Council to turn the Subway store at 16 Middleton Gardens into an adult gaming centre. It follows an application it submitted in July to turn the premises into a nail bar. That application has since been withdrawn. In the latest application, JR Planning said the Planning Inspectorate appeal which allowed Jeffries Casino to occupy the former Virgin Money premises at 20 Middleton Gardens had set a precedent for the change of use in a retail area. It said: “The Inspector found that the proposed adult gaming centre was likely to generate greater footfall over a typical day than many potential Class E uses. “The Inspector also found that the use would provide opportunities for linked trips to shops, pubs and other town centre businesses and make a modest contribution to the functioning of the centre. “It was concluded that the adult gaming centre would form part of a suitable mix of uses complementary to the retail role of Middleton town centre. Therefore, the vitality and viability of the centre would not be undermined. “The Inspector also considered the potential concentration of adult gaming centres. It was concluded that the establishment of an additional non-retail unit would not be materially harmful to the vitality and viability of the town centre.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Swindon Town are bracing themselves for fitness reports on three more players following their 1-0 defeat at Rochdale . Ian Holloway’s squad was down to the bare bones at the Crown Oil Arena, as Cian Hayes’ late header denied them a first away point since the opening day of the season . Swindon switched formation for the game to make a team around the available players, and there was not much help on the bench, with only James Debayo fully fit, and this was shown in the use of substitutions , as Town did not make a tactical switch until second-half stoppage time. Ollie Clarke was not initially meant to be in the squad, but he powered through a niggle and came on for Tom Nichols, who had gone down with a knock with around 25 minutes to play. Joseph Hungbo also had to be convinced to travel with the squad, as he was dealing with discomfort in his knee, but Holloway explained to him that he couldn’t lose anyone else, and so he played the final six minutes. But the possible casualties could have serious consequences for Swindon, as, along with Nichols, Aaron Drinan went down off the ball and was stretching out his hamstring before eventually being replaced, and Jack Thomson was also struggling with a cramp before he was replaced. Thomson and Drinan have been two of the players Town have relied on during this period, as both have played 90 minutes consistently. Who showed promise and who won the real duel?
